The card reads F Gantry Blanchard because the town's own directories print him so: Fergus 1843 has 'Blanchard, Francis Gurtrey, capitalist, res 45 Wells', Fergus 1839 'Blanchard, Francis G., real estate dealer, Lake street', Norris 1844 'Blanchard, Francis G.' — one man, forename Francis, middle name Gurtrey, which is the token this card carries as Gantry. The register spells the same man BLANCHARD F G, BLANCHARD F G AS, BLANCHARD FRANCIS G and BLANCHARD GURTREY, and every one of those is a reading of Francis Gurtrey. So the initial that fired the mechanical rule is not what carries the ruling: what carries it is a middle name the town prints out loud and the register repeats, on a surname the layer holds three of. The trade agrees too — a real estate dealer of 1839 is what a man who bought school-section town lots in the sale of October 1833 becomes, and that is a consistency rather than a proof. THE THING THIS RULING DOES NOT DECIDE: the residents layer holds a SECOND card, Gantry Blanchard, and on this reading the two are very likely one man. That is a duplicate-card question, filed as T-0993 beside T-0844's cluster of six; this ruling rules only that the register's F G is the card the crosswalk named.

The Democrat's letter list of 20 May 1835 prints 'Minard, Ira 2'; the register enters an Ira Minard on 161 acres in T40N R14E five weeks later, on 27 June 1835. Upholding here would be upholding a coincidence of date, which is the register telling us when somebody bought, not who. One further reading naming Ira Minard in the town would carry it.

REFUSED against L W Smith, on the same ground as SPENCER WILLIAM G under T-0700. The town's whole record of L W Smith is one line of the poll of 1834 — the card calls itself a projected resident, documented once and corroborated by nothing else — with no trade, no street, no second document and no entry in any of the three directories. The register offers LIMAN, and the very next row, ls0573, offers SIMAN for the same tract on the same day at a price one cent apart: the deposit itself does not know whether the man was a Lyman or a Simon, so the token the mechanical rule matched on is not stable in the source that supplies it. The register's row carries no middle initial at all, so the W — the one token that could discriminate among the eleven Smiths the layer holds — is checked against nothing. The COOK in the Residence column sits on the SIMAN reading, not this one, and Cook County in 1834 reaches far beyond the town. One row retracted, 140.18 acres in T38N R14E section 2.
